sections.h2: Where is Richardson County, and why is it unusual?
sections.html:
Richardson County is the southeast corner of Nebraska, and the lowest point in the state is on the Missouri River where it leaves Nebraska for Kansas and Missouri. The county covers 555 square miles, of which 552 are land. Missouri is across the river to the east and Kansas lies to the south.

Branches and tributaries of the Big Nemaha River flow southeast across rolling hills and empty into the Missouri at the county's southeast corner. Numerous drainages cut the land, and most of it is farmed. Parts of the Ioway and Sac and Fox reservations sit in the southeast corner between Falls City, Rulo and Hiawatha, Kansas, and the village of Preston is inside the Sac and Fox reservation. If a parcel is near that area, ask the assessor and a title company how it is classified before you list it.

sections.h2: How did Richardson County get its start?
sections.html:
The county was created in 1854, the year the Kansas-Nebraska Act opened the territory to settlement, and was reorganized in 1855 by the first territorial legislature. It was named for William A. Richardson, an Illinois congressman who sponsored the act and became governor of Nebraska Territory in 1858.

The first courthouse went up in 1863. A second one, built in 1873, burned on May 7, 1919. Falls City, founded in 1857 beside a rock ledge on the Big Nemaha called the Falls of Nemaha, won out over Salem after a prolonged contest and was declared the permanent county seat in 1860. Railroads then drove its growth: the Atchison and Nebraska arrived in 1871, the Missouri Pacific in 1882, and Falls City became a division point in 1909. Its population peaked at 6,200 in 1950.

sections.html:

With a median age of 47.2 and one in four residents 65 or older, some houses here will pass to heirs. An heir who lives in another state and inherits a house in a village such as Dawson, Stella or Verdon faces the same bill and the same deadlines as an owner next door.

sections.h2: Which towns and schools make up Richardson County?
sections.html:
Besides Falls City and Humboldt, the county has eight villages: Barada, Dawson, Preston, Rulo, Salem, Shubert, Stella and Verdon. Nim City and Strausville are unincorporated communities.

  • Falls City Public Schools, which runs two elementary schools, a junior high and Falls City High School
  • Humboldt Table Rock Steinauer Public Schools
  • Auburn Public Schools and Johnson-Brock Public Schools
  • Pawnee City Public Schools

Sacred Heart School in Falls City is a Catholic K to 12 school. The district a house falls in drives the school levy on the tax bill.

sections.h2: How do roads and the weather shape a Richardson County house?
sections.html:
U.S. Highways 73 and 75 run north and south through the county, U.S. 159 runs east to the Rulo bridge into Missouri, and Nebraska Highway 8 runs west along the southern border. Falls City itself has a hot-summer humid continental climate. Its July mean daily high is 88.1 degrees Fahrenheit, and the record high is 114.

Severe weather is part of the local record. On May 30, 1879, an F4 tornado, the Irving, Kansas tornado, crossed Richardson County on a path 800 yards wide and 100 miles long, killing 18 people and injuring 60. A single storm from over a century ago does not tell you much about your roof, but a hail or wind claim on file does, and buyers will ask about it.

sections.h2: Who bills Richardson County property tax?
sections.html:
The Richardson County Treasurer is at 1700 Stone Street, Room 105, Falls City, NE 68355, and takes questions at 402-245-3511. Real estate tax can be looked up and paid online through MIPS Inc., under an agreement with the county, for current and back taxes. The online fee is 2.35 percent on a card with a $2.00 minimum, or $1.00 for an e-check. Drainage taxes cannot be paid online.

The county's note about drainage taxes means they are billed in a way the online system does not handle, so ask the treasurer for the full balance, drainage items included, before you set a closing date.

sections.h2: What does the Richardson County Assessor do?
sections.html:
Kimberly Riggs is the county assessor, at 1700 Stone Street, Room 102, with a phone of 402-245-4012. The office is open 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. on weekdays, through lunch. It sets fair and equitable value on real and personal property, keeps parcel maps, prepares the tax roll for the treasurer, attends every Board of Equalization meeting and reviews applications for religious, charitable and educational exemptions and for homestead exemptions.

A protest goes on Form 422 to the County Clerk by June 30, one form per parcel, with your reasons, the value you want and documents the board can use to reach it. Statute 77-1502 says late or incomplete protests are dismissed. An owner who loses can go to the Tax Equalization and Review Commission by August 24.

sections.h2: How does the Richardson County tax sale work?
sections.html:
The county tax sale is held the first Monday in March at 9:00 a.m. at the courthouse, and the 2026 sale was March 2. The county advertises the delinquent list for three consecutive weeks in February and posts it online. It also posted a list of parcels that went unsold as of March 11, 2026.

  • Buyers register by the Friday before the sale and pay $25 to register.
  • The county charges $25 for each certificate sold.
  • The redemption period is three years, at 14 percent.
  • After three years without redemption, the buyer has six months to foreclose.

A parcel that did not sell is still delinquent. If yours appears on the unsold list, the tax is still owed and still needs a plan.

sections.h2: What should a Richardson County seller know about closing?
sections.html:
The title company gets the tax payoff from the treasurer, and the seller pays the documentary stamp tax collected by the register of deeds. The state rate is $3.32 per $1,000 of value for deeds recorded on or after July 18, 2026. Form 521 goes with the deed.

If the house is inherited, in disrepair or behind on taxes, tell us the address and parcel number and we will go through the numbers with you, with no obligation.

faqs.q: When are Richardson County property taxes delinquent?
faqs.a: The first half becomes delinquent May 1 and the second half September 1, under Nebraska Statute 77-204. Richardson is under the 100,000 population threshold that moves those dates earlier in Douglas, Lancaster and Sarpy counties.

faqs.q: Can I pay Richardson County taxes online?
faqs.a: Yes, through MIPS Inc., with a 2.35 percent card fee ($2.00 minimum) or a $1.00 e-check fee. Drainage taxes cannot be paid online, so call 402-245-3511.

faqs.q: Where do I file a protest in Richardson County?
faqs.a: File Form 422 with the County Clerk on or before June 30, one protest per parcel. The assessor, Kimberly Riggs, can be reached at 402-245-4012.

faqs.q: When is the Richardson County tax sale?
faqs.a: It is held the first Monday in March at 9:00 a.m. at the courthouse. The 2026 sale was March 2, with three weeks of advertising in February.

faqs.q: How long do I have to redeem after a tax sale in Richardson County?
faqs.a: The county's page gives three years. After that the certificate holder has six months to foreclose, and the certificates carry 14 percent interest.

faqs.q: Who pays the deed tax in a Richardson County sale?
faqs.a: The seller pays. Nebraska's documentary stamp tax is $3.32 for each $1,000 of value on deeds recorded from July 18, 2026.
